text: Two men who can manage anything the prairie asks of them, working a West that has maybe a decade of that work left in it. Pete and Big Boy ranch in the years just after the Second World War, and the film cares far more about what they are to each other than about what they do for a living. Stephen Frears directs from outside the tradition, a British filmmaker who treats horses and distance as labour rather than scenery and lets the cattle work pass without ceremony. Then romance enters, not as an event but as a pressure applied slowly to a friendship that has never had to explain itself. Neither man is equipped for that. What the 114 minutes are really spent on is talk: two hard-living men circling the one subject neither will name.

A Spanish film crew spends the civil war on a soundstage in Nazi Germany, at UFA's invitation, making a musical. Fernando Trueba plays it as comedy, the only register in which the arrangement holds: a troupe far from home, doing takes for hosts whose courtesy is a form of supervision. The war they left is elsewhere for the length of the picture, and that is exactly the pressure - their immediate problem is a shooting schedule, their larger one is that anything said between setups is heard by someone with an interest in it. Trueba spends 121 minutes on period sheen and lets the unease collect under the musical numbers. Nothing has to be denounced. The joke is that people this compromised are still arguing about lighting, and the performance at the centre of it took an acting prize at the European Film Awards.

A red flower pinned to a jacket so a stranger in a café will know who to look for. Cœurs gathers seven Parisians and the few rooms they keep passing through: a flat that is never large enough for the couple viewing it, an office where one colleague lends another videotapes, a bedroom where a bartender's father lies raging at the woman paid to sit with him. Nobody here is dramatically unhappy. They are unhappy at the scale of an evening. Alain Resnais, whose film took the critics' award at the European Film Academy, keeps the manners so even that feeling arrives sideways, in what people arrange rather than in what they say. Two hours pass by appointment - a viewing, a late shift, an advertisement answered on a Tuesday - and the suspense is entirely a question of who ends up in a room with whom.

Onofrio del Grillo has a title, an income and nothing to do with his afternoons, so he spends them making fools of people who are not free to object. Mario Monicelli sets him loose in an eighteenth-century Rome run by three authorities at once - his own class, the Pope, and a French occupation with plans for modernizing everybody - and the marquis works all three with the same appetite. The comedy is not gentle. A prank aimed upward is wit; the same prank aimed at a poor man is something else, and the film lets both land in the same afternoon so the difference is audible in the room. At 139 minutes there is time for the joke to sour and recover more than once. The lead performance took a David di Donatello, which is right: the picture is one man's timing and his refusal to be embarrassed.

Sara sees François on the street, he does not see her, and that is enough to loosen ten years of a settled life. Claire Denis keeps the arrangement almost embarrassingly plain: a couple in an apartment, a third man who belongs to both their histories, and a work proposal that gives him a reason to be there. Nothing stays hidden for long. The pressure comes from proximity instead - how two people who love each other talk once a third has been let back in, and how fast practised affection turns into something that has to be watched. Denis took the Silver Bear for direction, and the reason is legible in the handling: 117 minutes held at conversational distance, close enough that a change of tone registers before anyone will admit there has been one.

A travelling act works the Republican lines - songs, gags, whatever holds a room of tired soldiers for an hour. Carlos Saura hands the Spanish Civil War to performers rather than to soldiers, which changes what the war is: not a cause to die for but a series of audiences with different flags. Worn down by the front, the troupe sets out for Valencia, takes a wrong road and crosses into the other side's territory. From there the only thing they have to bargain with is the act itself. Timing becomes a survival skill rather than a talent, and the flattery a performer owes an audience acquires a very different weight. The film runs 102 minutes, carries the European Film Award for best film, and stays a comedy through most of that length, which is the harder choice: the gags have to keep working while the terms underneath them change.

A love story in which the woman is the older party, and the man's difficulty is not shyness but illness. The picture comes out of the American studio system in 1956, cut to the shape of a woman's melodrama, and then lets a second genre in through the side door: it is filed as mystery as often as romance, which says the question is not whether he loves her but what else is true about him. Robert Aldrich directs, and the material gives him something to push against - the illness stays a fact in the story rather than a decorative fragility. What the 107 minutes test is a woman who has built a small, self-sufficient life and now has to weigh how much of another person she can carry. The billing gives away the direction of travel. It gives away nothing about the price.

A music that Greece made in roughly the way America made the blues, and a singer young enough to have been formed by it rather than to have invented it. Rembetiko follows a group of players across the early decades of the twentieth century, which commits the film to the pace of a life rather than a plot - rooms, cities, whole years passing between songs. Costas Ferris keeps a woman at the centre of it, so each number arrives attached to what it costs her to perform, and the 110 minutes accumulate rather than build. It holds a Silver Bear, though nothing in it explains itself to an outsider. The songs are not translated into meaning. A viewer is expected to sit inside an idiom for a while before learning what it is for, and the film asks that without apology.

One dance hall, six decades of French history, and no plot to speak of - the film hands the whole job to couples crossing a floor to music. Ettore Scola keeps the camera in a single room from the 1920s to the 1980s and lets the country change around the furniture, so the waiter goes on serving while the clientele comes to include a collaborator, resistance fighters and, later, students with a cause. Faces recur, the music changes, the pairings rearrange. It is satire performed as choreography, which sounds like a stunt and is not, because the vocabulary of a dance floor - who is asked, who waits, who is watched from the wall - is already an account of a society. The Academy gave it the award for best international feature. The 112 minutes render a national century almost entirely in posture.

He goes up to the barricades with everyone else and does not throw the bottle, and the film treats that as the most interesting thing about him. Philippe Garrel gives the revolt a portion of the running time and the year afterwards nearly all of it: three hours of rooms, mostly at night, where François writes and talks and smokes and lets the days go. The money is Antoine's, an inheritance that pays for a flat and for the leisure to hold opinions in it. Lilie, who sculpts, keeps a job at a foundry. That difference sits under every conversation without once being argued, and it is the real subject - who can afford to go on believing, and for how long. The Louis Delluc Prize went to it, and across 183 minutes the film earns that the slow way, by staying in the room after the history has moved on.

A new girl arrives from Barcelona, and everything Celia has been taught to accept begins to look like something somebody decided. Celia is eleven, lives with her mother and attends a convent school in Zaragoza in the early 1990s, where the lessons about what a girl may know are delivered with total confidence. Brisa is not a rebellion; she is a second opinion, held by someone the same age. Pilar Palomero keeps the scale domestic - a classroom, a bedroom, a mother who answers some questions and closes others - and lets the friendship carry what a plot usually would. Nothing detonates. The pressure is cumulative: a rule that made sense last year, a silence at the kitchen table that starts to look like a decision. It took the Goya for best film, and its 97 minutes are largely what Celia notices before she has words for it.

A young woman goes looking for what her hometown did under the Nazis, and the town she grew up in turns on her for asking. Michael Verhoeven files this as comedy, and that decision is the whole strategy: the obstruction she meets is not sinister, it is municipal - procedures, delays, people who are terribly sorry but unable to help, a civic pride that hardens week by week. Guilt is not really the subject. The management of guilt is. The hostility is collective and entirely ordinary, which is the most uncomfortable thing the film has to propose. At 92 minutes, carrying an Academy Award for best international feature, it moves quickly enough to keep the joke from settling into a lecture. It was made in Germany about Germans, and the audience it implicates most directly was the one sitting in front of it.

In 1953 an American-backed coup moved through the streets of Iran, and four women made their separate ways to the same orchard garden. Shoja Azari films the history at an angle - the politics stay audible and mostly off to one side, while the foreground goes to what these women do with one another's company once they have it. The garden is not a symbol with a gate. It is a place with trees, walls and work, and its use is that nobody in it has to explain herself. The film is in Persian and was made from outside Iran, which shapes everything: 1953 has to be built for the camera rather than found, and every decision about how it looked was taken at a distance from it. A hundred minutes, four lives, one coup that none of them chose. Its direction carries a Silver Lion.

The designer of the prototype is the pilot's father-in-law, which makes every test flight in this film a family arrangement as much as an engineering one. David Lean made it in Britain in 1952, when passenger jets were about to become ordinary and the work of pushing an aeroplane past its limits still belonged to a handful of people who knew each other. The domestic half is not decoration. A father-in-law who needs the machine tested and a daughter who needs her husband alive are asking one person for opposite things, and the film keeps returning to the house between flights. It holds an Academy Award for sound, which is exact rather than decorative: the engine note is the instrument of tension here, and the 117 minutes are organized around the wait between runs.
